title: IoT Protocols Part 3: IoT Applications & Case Studies — Smart Home, Wearables, Smart City, Grid, Retail, Health, Car, Oil & Gas
description: Exam revision of IoT protocols, part 3: IoT applications across industries, the IoT applications ranking, and case studies: smart homes, wearables, smart city, smart parking, waste management, smart grid, smart retail, supply chain, connected health, life logging, connected car and IoT in the oil and gas industry.

scenes.title: IoT at businesses and society
lines: Where is the Internet of Things actually used?
Part three covers IoT at businesses and society: use cases and applications across industries.
Then the case studies: smart homes, wearables, smart cities, smart grid, retail, health, cars, and oil and gas.

scenes.title: Applications of IoT by sector
lines: Applications of IoT, sector by sector.
Consumer: smart home control of lighting, security and comfort, optimized energy use, and maintenance.
Retail: product tracking, inventory control, and focused marketing.
Medical: wearable devices, implanted devices, and telehealth services.
Military: resource allocation, threat analysis, and troop monitoring.
Industrial: smart meters, wear out sensing, manufacturing control, and climate control.
Automotive: parking, traffic flow, and anti theft location.
Environmental: species tracking, weather prediction, and resource management.
Agriculture: crop management, and soil analysis.

scenes.title: A few applications of IoT
lines: A few more applications of IoT:
building and home automation, manufacturing, the oil and gas sector,
medical and healthcare systems, media, and environmental monitoring,
infrastructure management, energy management, and transportation,
and a better quality of life for the elderly.
Plus wearable tech, smart appliances, and healthcare. You name it, and you will have it in IoT!

scenes.title: IoT to diverse applications
lines: IoT spreads into five big areas.
Home, the consumer: light bulbs, security, pet feeding, irrigation controller, smoke alarm, refrigerator, infotainment, washer and dryer, stove, and energy monitoring.
Transport, mobility: traffic routing, telematics, package monitoring, smart parking, insurance adjustments, supply chain, shipping, public transport, airlines and trains.
Health, the body: patient care, elderly monitoring, remote diagnostic, equipment monitoring, hospital hygiene, bio wearables, and food sensors.
Buildings, infrastructure: HVAC, security, lighting, electrical, transit, emergency alerts, structural integrity, occupancy, and energy credits.
Cities, industry: electrical distribution, maintenance, surveillance, signage, utilities and smart grid, emergency services, and waste management.

scenes.title: The IoT applications ranking
lines: The IoT applications ranking, by overall popularity.
Number one, smart home, at one hundred percent. Examples: smart thermostat, connected lights, smart fridge, smart door lock.
Two, wearables, sixty three percent: smart watch, activity tracker, smart glass.
Three, smart city, thirty four percent: smart parking and smart waste management.
Four, smart grid, twenty eight percent: smart metering. Five, industrial internet, twenty five percent: remote asset control.
Six, connected car, nineteen percent. Seven, connected health, six percent.
Eight, smart retail, two percent. Nine, smart supply chain, two percent. Ten, smart farming, one percent.
The scores came from monthly Google searches, tweets and LinkedIn posts, valid for the fourth quarter of 2014, from IoT Analytics.

scenes.title: Case study: smart homes
lines: Now the IoT case studies. First, smart homes.
A smart home connects lights and curtains, smart appliances, and smart media,
air control, background music, and central heating,
a safeguard security system, a video intercom, and central AC.

scenes.title: Case study: wearables
lines: Wearables are the second hot area in IoT.
Most of them are connected with smart phones.
Devices worn on the wrist, for example smart watches, like Samsung Gear.
Devices put on like a spectacle, for example Google Glass.
Smart garments.
And skin coloured tattoo or patch like sensors.

scenes.title: Wearable examples
lines: Some wearable examples.
Wearable panic buttons: built into jewellery or clothing, to quickly alert a circle of trusted contacts, and the police, when in distress.
Safe driving internables: ingestible pills with sensors that measure blood alcohol, and talk to your car, making it useless if you exceed the legal limit.
Smart garments: slow wash garments alert you when they need washing, saving water and energy. Exact measure garments send your body measurements to an app, which recommends clothes that fit.
Non verbal communication: Embrace, a smart garment that transfers physical touch wirelessly between couples.
And the mood detector: a skin coloured patch, or tattoo like sensor, that tracks your mood through the day and recommends actions.

scenes.title: Case study: smart city
lines: Smart city.
A smart city includes traffic management, water distribution, waste management, urban security, and environmental monitoring.
Many smart city solutions have promised to alleviate real pains of people living in cities these days.
IoT solutions in the smart city solve traffic congestion problems, reduce noise and pollution, and help make cities safer.
Smart city services include alert systems, security, connected cars, mobile centric services, public transit, and smart automation.
Smart parking: residents can identify and reserve the closest available space, traffic wardens can identify non compliant usage, and municipalities can introduce demand based pricing.

scenes.title: Smart waste management
lines: Efficient waste management in smart cities, supported by sensing as a service.
Garbage cans carry low cost passive sensors, or active sensors.
Garbage trucks act as data collectors.
The data goes to a cloud platform that supports sensing as a service.
It is then shared with the city council, recycling plants, manufacturing plants, and health and safety authorities.

scenes.title: Case study: smart grid
lines: Smart grid.
A smart grid uses information about the behaviours of electricity suppliers and consumers, in an automated fashion.
This technology helps to: one, deliver power more efficiently.
Two, improve operations. Three, reduce emissions and management costs.
Four, restore power failures faster.
The grid links homes, factories, nuclear, thermal and hydraulic power plants, photovoltaic, wind and renewable energy, ecological vehicles, and cities and offices.

scenes.title: Case study: smart retail
lines: Smart retail focuses on two areas: improving the customer experience, and optimizing supply chain operation.
An IoT shopping scenario. One: when entering the doors, scanners identify the tags on her clothing.
Two: when shopping in the market, the goods introduce themselves.
Three: when moving the goods, the reader tells the staff to put a new one on the shelf.
Four: when paying for the goods, the microchip of the credit card communicates with the checkout reader.

scenes.title: IoT solutions for supply chain
lines: IoT solutions for the supply chain.
Create fleet efficiencies, for optimization.
Life cycle visibility of the product.
Understand inventory levels and warehouse stock.
Study product performance, and predict failure.
And gain user insight.

scenes.title: Case study: connected health
lines: Connected health.
IoT in healthcare is a heterogeneous computing, wirelessly communicating system of apps and devices,
that connects patients and health providers to diagnose, monitor, track and store vital statistics and medical information.
Examples: headsets that measure brainwaves, clothes with sensing devices, BP monitors, glucose monitors, ECG monitors, and pulse oximeters.
Also sensors embedded in medical equipment, dispensing systems, surgical robots and device implants, and any wearable technology device.

scenes.title: Life logging
lines: IoT helps you in life logging.
How well do I sleep? A fitness band like the Fitbit Flex tracks sleep pattern, sleep efficiency, time asleep, and times awoken.
Can IoT help us know more about ourselves? Where you are going, who you interacted with, and how long you have spoken to friends.
The affinity of connections, how long it takes to get to work, the tone of your messages,
the amount you text, tweet or update, how much exercise you are getting, and how much you get distracted.

scenes.title: Case study: connected car
lines: Connected car.
Connected car applications can be separated into two categories.
One: in vehicle applications, inside a single car.
Two: V2V, vehicle to vehicle applications, where cars talk to each other.

scenes.title: Oil and gas industry introduction
lines: Finally, IoT in the oil and gas industry. It has three segments.
Upstream: exploration and production, E and P. Firms explore new hydrocarbon fields, and discovered fields are developed and petroleum produced.
Midstream: transportation of oil and natural gas, by shipping, pipelines, and LNG terminals.
Downstream: refinery processes crude oil to produce different products, in petrochemical plants, making polymers, plastics and other products.

scenes.title: Oil and gas: upstream
lines: The upstream industry problem.
It loses billions of dollars every year due to non productive time, NPT.
There are deadly accidents, and processes are not optimized.
The IoT solution: with IoT, refineries can plan their shutdowns, minimize their downtime, and improve safety records.
Accidents can be prevented, and processes can be optimized.

scenes.title: Oil and gas: midstream
lines: The midstream industry problem.
It has the challenging task of transporting variable volumes and grades of products, from multiple locations, to new end users and markets.
And of connecting pipeline networks, sensors, leak detection, alarms, and emergency shutdowns, to interact seamlessly.
The IoT solution: with IoT, data available for analysis and interpretation in real time would significantly reduce some of the major risks this sector deals with.

scenes.title: Oil and gas: downstream
lines: The downstream industry problem.
Refinery shutdowns, handling various grades of crude oil, and changing environmental regulations are pushing gross refining margins down to a bare minimum.
The IoT solution: with IoT, refineries can plan their shutdowns, minimize their downtime, and improve safety records.

scenes.title: Countless opportunities in oil and gas
lines: There are countless opportunities for IoT in oil and gas.

Upstream: asset tracking, vehicle monitoring, remote video, machine monitoring, site monitoring, well head monitoring, security and access sensors, lone worker tracking, rig monitoring, and tank monitoring.

Midstream: tank farm monitoring, field crew monitoring, remote video, pipeline monitoring, terminal access control, asset tracking, flow meter connectivity, wellhead monitoring, and cargo shipping monitoring.

Downstream: perimeter security sensors, perimeter video cameras, mobile asset tracking, vehicle monitoring, production sensors, IoT cloud storage, lone worker wearables, contractor tracking, and refinery monitoring.

scenes.title: Exam recap
lines: Quick recap.
Top of the ranking: smart home, then wearables, then smart city, smart grid, and industrial internet.
Smart grid helps four ways: efficient delivery, better operations, lower emissions and costs, faster restoration.
Smart retail: customer experience and supply chain. Connected car: in vehicle and V2V.
Oil and gas: upstream is exploration and production, midstream is transport, downstream is refining.
Good luck in your exam!
